title: Reinforcement Learning & Modern LLM Post-Training
blurb: MDPs, Q-learning, DQN, policy gradients, PPO, offline/imitation RL, then SFT, reward models, RLHF, DPO, GRPO and evaluation.
description: A full RL-to-LLM-alignment path modeled on Hugging Face Deep RL certification topics and current TRL post-training methods.

lessons.title: The reinforcement-learning interaction loop
objectives: Explain how an RL agent learns from interaction rather than labeled targets.
Explain how agent changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect agent with environment and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Reinforcement learning studies sequential decisions. At each step an agent observes state or observation, chooses an action, receives a reward, and reaches a new state.
lessons.explain: Reinforcement learning studies sequential decisions. At each step an agent observes state or observation, chooses an action, receives a reward, and reaches a new state.
commonMistakes: Treating reward as a label for each action ignores delayed effects and can encourage behavior that looks locally good but fails the long-term task.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: MDPs, states, actions & the Markov property
objectives: Specify an RL task as an MDP and identify when the observation is not truly Markov.
Explain how MDP changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect MDP with state and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An MDP formalizes states, actions, transition probabilities, reward function, and discount factor. The Markov property says the current state contains the information needed to predict the distribution of the next state given an action; history should not add information once state is known.
lessons.explain: An MDP formalizes states, actions, transition probabilities, reward function, and discount factor. The Markov property says the current state contains the information needed to predict the distribution of the next state given an action; history should not add information once state is known.
commonMistakes: Calling any sensor reading “the state” can violate the Markov assumption if past information is required to predict what happens next.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Returns, discounting & reward design
objectives: Compute discounted return and reason about reward design incentives.
Explain how return changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect return with discount factor and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The return is the cumulative future reward an agent tries to maximize. Discounting with gamma gives nearer rewards more weight and keeps infinite-horizon sums well behaved.
lessons.explain: The return is the cumulative future reward an agent tries to maximize. Discounting with gamma gives nearer rewards more weight and keeps infinite-horizon sums well behaved.
examples:
rewards=[0,1,2]; gamma=.9
G=sum((gamma**t)*r for t,r in enumerate(rewards))
print(round(G,3))
lessons.example:
rewards=[0,1,2]; gamma=.9
G=sum((gamma**t)*r for t,r in enumerate(rewards))
print(round(G,3))
commonMistakes: Adding a convenient shaping reward can create reward hacking where the agent maximizes the proxy instead of the real objective.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Value functions: V(s) and Q(s,a)
objectives: Interpret value functions as expected future return under a policy.
Explain how state value changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect state value with action value and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Vπ(s) is the expected return starting from state s and following policy π. Qπ(s,a) additionally conditions on taking action a first.
lessons.explain: Vπ(s) is the expected return starting from state s and following policy π. Qπ(s,a) additionally conditions on taking action a first.
commonMistakes: A value estimate is not an immediate reward; it summarizes expected future return and therefore depends on downstream behavior.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Bellman equations & bootstrapping
objectives: Explain how values relate recursively to reward plus next-state value.
Explain how Bellman equation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Bellman equation with bootstrapping and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Bellman equations express value as immediate reward plus discounted expected value of what follows. This recursive structure enables dynamic programming and temporal-difference learning.
lessons.explain: Bellman equations express value as immediate reward plus discounted expected value of what follows. This recursive structure enables dynamic programming and temporal-difference learning.
commonMistakes: Bootstrapping from a badly biased value target can spread that bias through many states, so stability and target construction matter.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Dynamic programming: policy evaluation & iteration
objectives: Solve small known MDPs when transition and reward models are available.
Explain how policy evaluation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect policy evaluation with policy improvement and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Dynamic programming repeatedly applies Bellman backups using a known environment model. Policy evaluation estimates values for a fixed policy; policy improvement chooses better actions using those values; policy iteration alternates both.
lessons.explain: Dynamic programming repeatedly applies Bellman backups using a known environment model. Policy evaluation estimates values for a fixed policy; policy improvement chooses better actions using those values; policy iteration alternates both.
commonMistakes: Dynamic programming assumes access to transition probabilities and rewards; applying it directly to an unknown real environment is usually impossible.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Monte Carlo learning
objectives: Estimate values from complete sampled episodes without an environment model.
Explain how Monte Carlo changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Monte Carlo with episode and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Monte Carlo methods wait until an episode ends, compute the observed return, and use it as a target. They do not bootstrap and need no transition model, making them conceptually simple and unbiased with enough representative samples.
lessons.explain: Monte Carlo methods wait until an episode ends, compute the observed return, and use it as a target. They do not bootstrap and need no transition model, making them conceptually simple and unbiased with enough representative samples.
commonMistakes: Treating one noisy episode return as a reliable value estimate produces unstable learning; Monte Carlo relies on averaging many samples.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Temporal-difference learning
objectives: Update a value estimate before an episode finishes.
Explain how TD learning changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect TD learning with TD error and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Temporal-difference learning combines sampling with bootstrapping. TD(0) updates V(s) toward r + γV(s′) after each transition, using the TD error as the learning signal.
lessons.explain: Temporal-difference learning combines sampling with bootstrapping. TD(0) updates V(s) toward r + γV(s′) after each transition, using the TD error as the learning signal.
examples:
V=2.0; reward=1; next_v=3; gamma=.9; alpha=.1
td=reward+gamma*next_v-V
V += alpha*td
print(V)
lessons.example:
V=2.0; reward=1; next_v=3; gamma=.9; alpha=.1
td=reward+gamma*next_v-V
V += alpha*td
print(V)
commonMistakes: Using too large a learning rate can make bootstrapped value estimates oscillate or diverge instead of settling.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: SARSA & Q-learning
objectives: Contrast on-policy and off-policy TD control.
Explain how SARSA changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect SARSA with Q-learning and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: SARSA updates Q using the next action actually chosen by the current behavior policy, so it is on-policy. Q-learning updates toward the maximum next-action value, learning a greedy target policy while behavior may still explore, so it is off-policy.
lessons.explain: SARSA updates Q using the next action actually chosen by the current behavior policy, so it is on-policy. Q-learning updates toward the maximum next-action value, learning a greedy target policy while behavior may still explore, so it is off-policy.
examples:
q_sa=1; r=0; gamma=.9; q_next_actual=.5; q_next_best=1.2
print("SARSA target",r+gamma*q_next_actual,"Q target",r+gamma*q_next_best)
lessons.example:
q_sa=1; r=0; gamma=.9; q_next_actual=.5; q_next_best=1.2
print("SARSA target",r+gamma*q_next_actual,"Q target",r+gamma*q_next_best)
commonMistakes: Assuming on-policy and off-policy methods behave identically can hide important safety differences in environments where exploration has consequences.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Exploration: ε-greedy, schedules & uncertainty
objectives: Balance gathering information with using the best-known action.
Explain how exploration changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect exploration with epsilon-greedy and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An RL agent must explore because current value estimates may be wrong. ε-greedy chooses a random action with probability ε and the greedy action otherwise; schedules often reduce ε as knowledge improves.
lessons.explain: An RL agent must explore because current value estimates may be wrong. ε-greedy chooses a random action with probability ε and the greedy action otherwise; schedules often reduce ε as knowledge improves.
examples:
import random
actions=["left","right"]; epsilon=.1
choice=random.choice(actions) if random.random()<epsilon else "right"
print(choice)
lessons.example:
import random
actions=["left","right"]; epsilon=.1
choice=random.choice(actions) if random.random()<epsilon else "right"
print(choice)
commonMistakes: Decaying exploration too quickly can lock the agent into a mediocre policy based on early noisy experience.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Function approximation & neural value models
objectives: Generalize value estimates to large or continuous state spaces.
Explain how function approximation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect function approximation with generalization and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Tabular values require a separate entry for every state-action pair, which is impossible in large spaces. Function approximation predicts values or policies from features using linear models or neural networks.
lessons.explain: Tabular values require a separate entry for every state-action pair, which is impossible in large spaces. Function approximation predicts values or policies from features using linear models or neural networks.
examples:
def q(features,weights): return sum(x*w for x,w in zip(features,weights))
print(q([1,.5],[.4,1.2]))
lessons.example:
def q(features,weights): return sum(x*w for x,w in zip(features,weights))
print(q([1,.5],[.4,1.2]))
commonMistakes: A function approximator can generalize in the wrong direction, so lower training loss does not automatically mean a better policy.

lessons.title: Deep Q-Networks: replay & target networks
objectives: Explain the two major stability mechanisms in DQN.
Explain how DQN changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect DQN with replay buffer and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: DQN uses a neural network to approximate Q values. Consecutive environment transitions are correlated, so replay buffers randomize training batches and reuse experience.
lessons.explain: DQN uses a neural network to approximate Q values. Consecutive environment transitions are correlated, so replay buffers randomize training batches and reuse experience.
commonMistakes: Training only on the newest transition couples updates strongly to recent trajectory order and can destabilize the network.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Policy gradients & REINFORCE
objectives: Optimize policy parameters directly using sampled returns.
Explain how policy gradient changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect policy gradient with REINFORCE and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Policy-gradient methods parameterize the action distribution and adjust parameters to increase the log-probability of actions that produced high return. REINFORCE is the basic Monte Carlo policy-gradient estimator.
lessons.explain: Policy-gradient methods parameterize the action distribution and adjust parameters to increase the log-probability of actions that produced high return. REINFORCE is the basic Monte Carlo policy-gradient estimator.
examples:
advantages=[1.2,-.4,.7]
log_probs=[-.2,-1.0,-.5]
loss=-sum(a*lp for a,lp in zip(advantages,log_probs))
print(round(loss,3))
lessons.example:
advantages=[1.2,-.4,.7]
log_probs=[-.2,-1.0,-.5]
loss=-sum(a*lp for a,lp in zip(advantages,log_probs))
print(round(loss,3))
commonMistakes: Using raw returns without normalization or a baseline can produce very noisy gradients that require many trajectories.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Actor-critic methods & advantage estimation
objectives: Use a learned critic to reduce policy-gradient variance.
Explain how actor-critic changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect actor-critic with critic and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Actor-critic methods learn a policy actor and a value critic together. The critic estimates expected return and the actor updates using an advantage signal that compares an action’s outcome with what was expected.
lessons.explain: Actor-critic methods learn a policy actor and a value critic together. The critic estimates expected return and the actor updates using an advantage signal that compares an action’s outcome with what was expected.
commonMistakes: A poor critic can provide misleading advantages and push the policy in the wrong direction even when the policy optimizer is implemented correctly.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: PPO: clipped policy optimization
objectives: Explain how PPO limits destructive policy updates while reusing sampled data.
Explain how PPO changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect PPO with importance ratio and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: PPO compares the probability of sampled actions under the new and old policies using an importance ratio. Its clipped objective limits the incentive to move the ratio too far from 1, reducing the chance that one optimization phase destroys the policy.
lessons.explain: PPO compares the probability of sampled actions under the new and old policies using an importance ratio. Its clipped objective limits the incentive to move the ratio too far from 1, reducing the chance that one optimization phase destroys the policy.
commonMistakes: Treating PPO as automatically stable and ignoring KL divergence, reward curves, or entropy can allow silent policy collapse.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Offline RL & distribution shift
objectives: Reason about learning from a fixed dataset without collecting new interaction.
Explain how offline RL changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect offline RL with behavior policy and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Offline RL learns from transitions collected by a behavior policy and cannot correct mistakes by immediately gathering new data. The major challenge is distribution shift: the learned policy may choose actions that are poorly represented in the dataset, where value estimates are unreliable.
lessons.explain: Offline RL learns from transitions collected by a behavior policy and cannot correct mistakes by immediately gathering new data. The major challenge is distribution shift: the learned policy may choose actions that are poorly represented in the dataset, where value estimates are unreliable.
commonMistakes: A high predicted Q value for an action rarely seen in the offline data may be extrapolation error rather than evidence that the action is actually good.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Imitation learning & behavior cloning
objectives: Learn a policy from demonstrations and understand compounding error.
Explain how imitation learning changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect imitation learning with behavior cloning and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Behavior cloning treats expert state-action pairs as supervised learning examples. It is simple and useful when expert demonstrations are abundant, but the learned policy may visit states absent from the expert dataset; small errors can compound because the model then acts on unfamiliar inputs.
lessons.explain: Behavior cloning treats expert state-action pairs as supervised learning examples. It is simple and useful when expert demonstrations are abundant, but the learned policy may visit states absent from the expert dataset; small errors can compound because the model then acts on unfamiliar inputs.
commonMistakes: Evaluating only on expert-distribution states can hide the compounding-error problem that appears when the learned policy makes its own mistakes.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Multi-agent reinforcement learning
objectives: Explain why learning becomes harder when other agents also change their policies.
Explain how multi-agent RL changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect multi-agent RL with non-stationarity and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: In multi-agent RL, the effective environment seen by one learner changes as other agents learn, breaking the stationarity assumption used by many single-agent methods. Tasks may be cooperative, competitive, or mixed.
lessons.explain: In multi-agent RL, the effective environment seen by one learner changes as other agents learn, breaking the stationarity assumption used by many single-agent methods. Tasks may be cooperative, competitive, or mixed.
commonMistakes: Training against only one fixed opponent can produce a brittle policy that overfits that opponent rather than learning a robust strategy.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: RL evaluation, seeds & reproducibility
objectives: Evaluate policies across episodes, seeds, and meaningful baselines.
Explain how evaluation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect evaluation with random seed and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: RL results are noisy because exploration, initialization, environment randomness, and data order all matter. A credible evaluation reports performance across multiple seeds or runs, separates training and evaluation behavior, includes simple baselines, and examines variance and failure modes—not just the best checkpoint.
lessons.explain: RL results are noisy because exploration, initialization, environment randomness, and data order all matter. A credible evaluation reports performance across multiple seeds or runs, separates training and evaluation behavior, includes simple baselines, and examines variance and failure modes—not just the best checkpoint.
commonMistakes: Reporting only the best seed or the highest single episode return can make an unstable method look reliably strong.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Instruction datasets & chat templates
objectives: Prepare conversational training data with consistent roles, formatting, and quality controls.
Explain how instruction data changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect instruction data with chat template and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: LLM post-training begins with data design. Instruction examples define the behavior you want: system constraints, user requests, assistant responses, tool traces, or reasoning-style outputs depending on the objective.
lessons.explain: LLM post-training begins with data design. Instruction examples define the behavior you want: system constraints, user requests, assistant responses, tool traces, or reasoning-style outputs depending on the objective.
commonMistakes: Mixing incompatible chat templates or role conventions can teach the model formatting artifacts and cause inference-time prompt mismatch.

lessons.title: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
objectives: Adapt a pretrained language model to desired response patterns using labeled examples.
Explain how SFT changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect SFT with teacher forcing and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: SFT continues next-token training on curated instruction/response data. The model is typically trained with teacher forcing while masking tokens that should not contribute to the objective, such as parts of the prompt depending on the recipe.
lessons.explain: SFT continues next-token training on curated instruction/response data. The model is typically trained with teacher forcing while masking tokens that should not contribute to the objective, such as parts of the prompt depending on the recipe.
commonMistakes: Training too long on a narrow SFT dataset can overfit style, reduce general capabilities, or make the model less robust outside the training distribution.

lessons.title: Preference data & reward modeling
objectives: Train or use a model that scores which of two responses better matches human preferences.
Explain how preference data changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect preference data with reward model and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Preference datasets contain comparisons such as chosen versus rejected responses for the same prompt. A reward model learns a scalar preference signal from those pairs and can guide RLHF.
lessons.explain: Preference datasets contain comparisons such as chosen versus rejected responses for the same prompt. A reward model learns a scalar preference signal from those pairs and can guide RLHF.
commonMistakes: Treating preference labels as objective truth hides annotator disagreement and reward-model biases that can shape downstream behavior.

lessons.title: RLHF with PPO
objectives: Connect a reward model, reference policy, and PPO-style policy update.
Explain how RLHF changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect RLHF with reward model and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Classic RLHF treats the language model as a policy that generates responses, scores them with a reward model, and updates the policy with PPO while constraining drift from a reference model, commonly through a KL penalty.
lessons.explain: Classic RLHF treats the language model as a policy that generates responses, scores them with a reward model, and updates the policy with PPO while constraining drift from a reference model, commonly through a KL penalty.
examples:
reward=1.8; kl=.3; beta=.2
objective=reward-beta*kl
print("regularized reward",objective)
lessons.example:
reward=1.8; kl=.3; beta=.2
objective=reward-beta*kl
print("regularized reward",objective)
commonMistakes: Maximizing reward-model score without controlling policy drift can produce reward hacking and outputs far from the base model distribution.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
objectives: Understand preference optimization without an explicit learned reward model plus online RL loop.
Explain how DPO changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect DPO with preference optimization and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: DPO converts pairwise preference learning into a supervised-style objective comparing how strongly the current policy versus a reference model prefers chosen responses over rejected ones. This removes the explicit reward-model/PPO loop from the basic pipeline and is widely used because it is simpler operationally.
lessons.explain: DPO converts pairwise preference learning into a supervised-style objective comparing how strongly the current policy versus a reference model prefers chosen responses over rejected ones. This removes the explicit reward-model/PPO loop from the basic pipeline and is widely used because it is simpler operationally.
examples:
pairs=[("chosen A","rejected A"),("chosen B","rejected B")]
print("preference pairs",len(pairs))
lessons.example:
pairs=[("chosen A","rejected A"),("chosen B","rejected B")]
print("preference pairs",len(pairs))
commonMistakes: Calling DPO “RLHF without any trade-offs” ignores sensitivity to data quality, reference model choice, and the possibility of over-optimizing a narrow preference distribution.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: GRPO, RLOO, KTO & modern post-training variants
objectives: Recognize why different post-training objectives exist and when their assumptions differ.
Explain how GRPO changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect GRPO with RLOO and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Modern post-training libraries provide several objectives because tasks, feedback types, and compute constraints differ. GRPO uses relative rewards within sampled groups and is popular in reasoning-oriented online training; RLOO uses leave-one-out baselines to reduce variance; KTO can learn from desirable/undesirable examples rather than explicit pairs.
lessons.explain: Modern post-training libraries provide several objectives because tasks, feedback types, and compute constraints differ. GRPO uses relative rewards within sampled groups and is popular in reasoning-oriented online training; RLOO uses leave-one-out baselines to reduce variance; KTO can learn from desirable/undesirable examples rather than explicit pairs.
examples:
rewards=[1.0,0.2,1.8,.6]
mean=sum(rewards)/len(rewards)
relative=[round(r-mean,2) for r in rewards]
print(relative)
lessons.example:
rewards=[1.0,0.2,1.8,.6]
mean=sum(rewards)/len(rewards)
relative=[round(r-mean,2) for r in rewards]
print(relative)
commonMistakes: Switching algorithms because one is fashionable without matching its feedback format and evaluation protocol can make training harder to interpret, not better.

lessons.title: Post-training evaluation, safety & end-to-end pipeline

Connect post-training evaluation with safety and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: A complete post-training system includes dataset versioning, SFT or preference stages, reproducible configs, checkpoint management, automated evaluations, human review, safety checks, and regression gates against the base or previous production model.
lessons.explain: A complete post-training system includes dataset versioning, SFT or preference stages, reproducible configs, checkpoint management, automated evaluations, human review, safety checks, and regression gates against the base or previous production model.
commonMistakes: Shipping because the training loss or preference reward improved can hide regressions in unrelated capabilities or safety behavior.
